Scalars and Vectors.intro: Physical quantities can be either scalar (magnitude only) or vector (magnitude and direction). This distinction is fundamental to understanding forces.
Scalars and Vectors.mnemonic: "Vectors have Direction — think of a VD satnav" — Velocity, Displacement, force, acceleration, momentum are Vectors (all need a direction). Speed, Distance, mass, energy, temperature are Scalars.

sections.title: Scalars vs Vectors
sections.text: All physical quantities are either scalars (magnitude only) or vectors (magnitude and direction). Many quantities come in scalar/vector pairs.
points: Scalar — magnitude only: speed, distance, mass, energy, temperature, time, pressure
Vector — magnitude AND direction: velocity, displacement, force, acceleration, momentum, weight
Scalar/vector pairs — speed (scalar) & velocity (vector); distance (scalar) & displacement (vector)
Representing vectors — drawn as arrows; arrow length = magnitude; arrow direction = direction of quantity
Negative vectors — a negative value indicates the opposite direction (e.g. −5 m/s means 5 m/s in the reverse direction)

sections.title: Adding Vectors
sections.text: When combining vectors, direction must be taken into account. Vectors in opposite directions partially cancel.
points: Same direction — add magnitudes: two 5 N forces in same direction = 10 N resultant
Opposite directions — subtract magnitudes: 8 N right + 3 N left = 5 N right
At right angles — use Pythagoras: resultant² = a² + b²; use trigonometry for direction
Scale drawing — draw vectors tip-to-tail; resultant = line from start to end; measure length and angle
Equilibrium — when resultant of all forces = 0, object is in equilibrium (no acceleration)

sections.title: Free Body Diagrams
sections.text: Free body diagrams show all the forces acting on an object as arrows, helping to find the resultant force.
points: Free body diagram — arrows showing all forces on a single object; arrow length proportional to magnitude
Labelling — each arrow must be labelled with the force name and value (e.g. Weight = 500 N downward)
Resultant force — the single vector that replaces all forces; determines acceleration by F = ma
Balanced forces — arrows of equal length in opposite directions; resultant = 0; object in equilibrium
Unbalanced forces — arrows unequal; object accelerates in direction of resultant

keyTerms.def: A quantity with magnitude only — no direction (e.g. speed, mass, temperature)
A quantity with both magnitude and direction (e.g. velocity, force, acceleration)
The single vector that has the same effect as two or more vectors combined
Distance travelled in a specified direction from a starting point — a vector quantity
State where the resultant of all forces is zero — object is stationary or moving at constant velocity
A diagram showing all forces acting on a single object as labelled arrows

examTips: Speed is scalar; velocity is vector. Distance is scalar; displacement is vector. AQA regularly asks students to classify quantities — memorise all common examples.
When forces are balanced (resultant = 0), the object is in equilibrium — it could be stationary OR moving at constant velocity. Do not say it must be stationary.
For vectors at right angles, use Pythagoras to find magnitude: resultant² = a² + b². Use tan(θ) = opposite/adjacent to find the angle.
commonMistakes: Saying speed and velocity are the same — velocity has a specific direction, speed does not. A car going around a roundabout at constant speed has changing velocity.
Forgetting to state direction when describing a vector quantity — '10 m/s' is speed; '10 m/s north' is velocity.
Adding vector magnitudes regardless of direction — vectors in opposite directions must be subtracted, not added.
clozePassages: A scalar quantity has only magnitude (size). Examples include speed, distance, mass, temperature, and energy. A vector quantity has both magnitude and direction. Examples include velocity, displacement, force, acceleration, and momentum. The difference is important — a car travelling at 30 m/s north has a different velocity from one travelling at 30 m/s south, even though both have the same speed.

Vector quantities can be represented by arrows — the length of the arrow shows the magnitude and the direction of the arrow shows the direction. When adding vectors in the same direction, the magnitudes simply add. When vectors are in opposite directions, they subtract. For vectors at other angles, the resultant can be found by drawing a scale diagram. Two forces can be combined to find a single resultant force.

The resultant force is the single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting on an object combined. If the resultant force is zero, the forces are balanced and the object is in equilibrium. If the resultant force is non-zero, it is an unbalanced force and will cause the object to accelerate. Force diagrams (free body diagrams) show all the forces acting on an object with arrows indicating direction and magnitude.

Forces.intro: Forces are pushes or pulls that can change the speed, direction or shape of an object. Understanding forces and their effects is central to P5.
Forces.mnemonic: "Weight = mg: Wimpy mice get weighed" — W = mg. On Earth, g = 9.8 N/kg (use 10 N/kg for estimates). Weight is a Force (newtons), not mass (kilograms).

sections.title: Contact and Non-Contact Forces
sections.text: Forces are either contact forces (require physical touching) or non-contact forces (act at a distance through fields).
points: Contact forces — friction, normal (contact) force, tension, air resistance (drag), upthrust
Non-contact forces — gravity (weight), magnetic force, electrostatic force
Normal force — perpendicular to surface; stops objects passing through each other
Tension — pulling force in a rope, string or cable; acts along the rope
Friction — always opposes relative motion; converts kinetic energy to thermal energy

sections.title: Resultant Force
sections.text: The resultant force is the vector sum of all forces on an object. It determines whether the object accelerates.
points: Balanced forces — resultant = 0; object stays at rest OR moves at constant velocity (Newton's 1st law)
Unbalanced forces — resultant ≠ 0; object accelerates in direction of resultant (Newton's 2nd law)
Terminal velocity — when drag = driving force; resultant = 0; object moves at constant velocity
Free body diagram — shows all forces on object; resultant found by vector addition
Resolving forces — splitting a force into horizontal and vertical components using trigonometry

sections.title: Weight and Mass
sections.text: Weight and mass are different quantities. Weight is the gravitational force on an object; mass is the amount of matter.

callout.label: Formula
callout.text: W = m × g (Weight = mass × gravitational field strength). On Earth, g = 9.8 N/kg. Weight is a FORCE (newtons); mass is an amount of matter (kilograms).

points: W = mg — weight (N) = mass (kg) × gravitational field strength (N/kg)
g on Earth — 9.8 N/kg (≈ 10 N/kg for estimates); g on Moon ≈ 1.6 N/kg
Worked example — 60 kg person: W = 60 × 9.8 = 588 N on Earth; 60 × 1.6 = 96 N on Moon
Mass is constant — does not change with location; weight changes because g changes
Centre of gravity — the point where the weight of an object appears to act

keyTerms.def: A push or pull that can change an object's speed, direction or shape — measured in newtons (N)
The gravitational force on an object: W = mg, measured in newtons (N)
The single force that represents the combined effect of all forces on an object
State where all forces are balanced (resultant = 0) — no acceleration
Contact force opposing relative motion between surfaces — converts KE to thermal energy
Constant velocity reached when drag force equals driving force — zero resultant, zero acceleration

examTips: Weight = mg. On Earth, g = 9.8 N/kg (use 10 N/kg for estimates). AQA papers will specify which value to use. Remember: weight is in newtons, mass is in kilograms — never mix them up.
Balanced forces do NOT mean no forces are acting. Balanced means zero RESULTANT force. The object can still be moving — at constant velocity.
Friction always acts opposite to the direction of motion or tendency of motion. It never acts in the same direction as movement.
commonMistakes: Confusing mass (kg, constant) and weight (N, depends on gravitational field strength) — an astronaut on the Moon has the same mass but less weight.
Saying balanced forces mean the object is stationary — it could be moving at constant velocity. Only an UNBALANCED force causes acceleration.
Saying friction acts in the direction of motion — friction ALWAYS opposes motion or the tendency to move.
clozePassages: A force is a push or pull that can change the shape, speed, or direction of an object. Forces are measured in newtons (N). Contact forces include friction, normal contact force, and tension. Non-contact forces include gravity, electrostatic force, and magnetic force. Forces always come in pairs — Newton's third law states that every action has an equal and opposite reaction.

Weight is the force of gravity on an object and acts downward towards the centre of the Earth. It is calculated as W = mg, where m is mass in kg and g is gravitational field strength (10 N/kg on Earth). Mass is the amount of matter in an object and does not change with location. Weight changes with gravitational field strength — an object weighs less on the Moon than on Earth because the Moon's gravitational field is weaker.

When two surfaces are in contact and one moves relative to the other, friction acts opposing motion. Friction converts kinetic energy to thermal energy. Air resistance (drag) acts on objects moving through air. The magnitude of drag increases with speed. When drag equals the driving force on a falling object, it reaches terminal velocity — a constant speed where forces are balanced and acceleration is zero.

Work Done.intro: Work is done when a force causes an object to move. It is a measure of energy transferred.
Work Done.mnemonic: "Work = Force × Distance; Powerful Workers Do it Fast" — W = Fd, and Power P = W/t. A 'powerful' worker does the same job in less time.

sections.title: Work Done Formula
sections.text: Work done equals energy transferred. It depends on the force applied and the distance moved in the direction of the force.

callout.label: Formula
callout.text: W = F × d (Work done = Force × distance moved in direction of force). Units: joules (J). 1 J = 1 N × 1 m.

points: W = Fd — work done (J) = force (N) × distance (m) in direction of force
Work done = energy transferred — they are numerically identical and have the same unit (joules)
No movement = no work — holding a heavy box stationary does NO work (no displacement)
Perpendicular force — no work done if force is at 90° to displacement (e.g. gravity on horizontal motion)
Worked example — pushing 200 N force over 5 m: W = 200 × 5 = 1000 J

sections.title: Power
sections.text: Power is the rate of doing work or the rate of energy transfer. A more powerful machine does the same work in less time.

callout.label: Power Formula
callout.text: P = W/t (Power = Work done ÷ time). Units: watts (W). Also P = Fv (Power = Force × velocity).

points: P = W/t — power (W) = work done (J) ÷ time (s); 1 watt = 1 joule per second
P = Fv — power = force × velocity; useful when force and speed are given
Worked example — 600 J done in 3 s: P = 600 ÷ 3 = 200 W
Units — power in watts (W) or kilowatts (kW); 1 kW = 1000 W
High power — does more work per second; same total work in less time

sections.title: Work Done Against Gravity
sections.text: When an object is lifted, work is done against gravity and stored as gravitational potential energy.
points: GPE = mgh — gravitational potential energy (J) = mass (kg) × g (N/kg) × height (m)
Work done lifting = GPE gained — W = mgh (assuming no energy lost to friction or air resistance)
Worked example — lifting 5 kg box by 2 m: W = 5 × 9.8 × 2 = 98 J
Ramp vs vertical lift — same work done against gravity either way; ramp reduces force needed but increases distance
Energy conservation — total energy is always conserved; work done = useful energy out + wasted energy

keyTerms.def: Energy transferred when a force moves an object in the direction of the force: W = Fd (joules)
Rate of doing work or energy transfer: P = W/t (watts)
Unit of energy and work — 1 J = 1 N × 1 m; energy transferred when 1 N force moves 1 m
Unit of power — 1 W = 1 J/s; 1 watt means 1 joule of work done per second
Energy stored by an object due to its height in a gravitational field: GPE = mgh
Ratio of useful energy output to total energy input; always less than 1 (100%) due to energy losses

examTips: Work done = energy transferred — they are equivalent. AQA may ask you to calculate one when given information for the other.
P = W/t and P = Fv are both on the formula sheet — choose the one that matches the given data. If you know force and velocity, use P = Fv directly.
No movement = no work done. A person holding a heavy bag stationary does no work on the bag (no displacement in direction of force).
commonMistakes: Forgetting that work requires movement — a force applied without displacement does zero work, even if the person feels tired.
Using total distance instead of distance in the direction of the force — if a force acts at an angle to displacement, only the component in the direction of motion counts.
Confusing work (J) and power (W) — work is energy transferred; power is the rate at which work is done.
clozePassages: Work done is the energy transferred when a force causes an object to move in the direction of the force. The formula is: W = Fs, where F is force in newtons and s is distance in metres. Work done is measured in joules (J). One joule of work is done when a force of one newton moves an object one metre in the direction of the force. Work done equals the energy transferred to the object.

The work done against gravity when lifting an object equals its gain in gravitational potential energy: W = mgh. When a force acts on an object and causes it to move in the direction of the force, the work done equals the gain in kinetic energy (assuming no friction). In practice, some work is done against friction and is converted to thermal energy. The principle of conservation of energy still applies — total energy is conserved.

Power is the rate of doing work — the amount of work done per second. P = W/t, where W is work done in joules and t is time in seconds. Power is measured in watts (W). A more powerful engine can do the same work in less time, or more work in the same time. Efficiency relates useful work output to total work input. Reducing friction and air resistance increases efficiency by reducing unwanted energy transfers.

Elasticity.intro: Elastic materials return to their original shape after a force is removed. Hooke's Law describes the relationship between force and extension.
Elasticity.mnemonic: "Force = k × extension: Fairly knobbly elastic" — F = ke. A stiffer spring has a larger k value. Remember: 'Elastic energy = half k e squared': Ee = ½ke².

sections.title: Hooke's Law
sections.text: Hooke's Law states that extension is directly proportional to force, up to the limit of proportionality.

callout.label: Formula
callout.text: F = k × e (Force = spring constant × extension). Spring constant k is in N/m. Hooke's Law applies up to the LIMIT OF PROPORTIONALITY.

points: F = ke — force (N) = spring constant (N/m) × extension (m)
Spring constant k — measures stiffness; larger k = stiffer spring; gradient of F-e graph
Proportional region — straight line through origin on F-e graph; extension ∝ force
Limit of proportionality — point beyond which F-e graph curves; Hooke's Law no longer applies
Worked example — spring with k = 40 N/m, force = 8 N: extension = F/k = 8/40 = 0.2 m

sections.title: Elastic and Inelastic Deformation
sections.text: Materials can undergo elastic deformation (reversible) or inelastic deformation (permanent) depending on the force applied.
points: Elastic deformation — returns to original shape and size when force removed; no permanent change
Inelastic (plastic) deformation — does not return to original shape; permanently changed; beyond elastic limit
Elastic potential energy stored — Ee = ½ke² (energy stored in a stretched or compressed spring)
Energy conversion — when released, elastic PE converts to kinetic energy
Elastic limit — maximum extension for elastic behaviour; beyond this, material is permanently deformed

sections.title: Investigating Hooke's Law
sections.text: The spring constant can be measured experimentally by recording the extension for different loads and plotting a force-extension graph.
points: Method — hang masses on spring; measure natural length; record extension for each mass added
Graph — plot force (y-axis) against extension (x-axis); gradient = spring constant k
Reading off k — k = ΔF/Δe = gradient of the straight-line portion
Beyond elastic limit — line curves; spring does not return to original length when masses removed
Safety — clamp stand securely; use eye protection; do not add masses beyond elastic limit

keyTerms.def: Extension is proportional to force: F = ke — valid only up to the limit of proportionality
Measure of stiffness of a spring: k = F/e, measured in N/m — higher k = stiffer spring
Reversible deformation — object returns to original shape when force is removed
Point beyond which Hooke's Law no longer applies — force and extension are no longer proportional
Energy stored in a stretched or compressed elastic object: Ee = ½ke²
Permanent deformation — object does not return to its original shape after force is removed

examTips: F = ke — on the AQA formula sheet. The gradient of a force-extension graph equals the spring constant k. Steeper gradient = larger k = stiffer spring.
Elastic potential energy: Ee = ½ke² — also on the formula sheet. The extension must be in metres when using this formula.

Elastic means it RETURNS to original shape; inelastic (plastic) means permanent deformation. 'Elastic' does NOT mean stretchy — rubber can be elastic and spring steel can be inelastic if overstretched.
commonMistakes: Saying elastic means stretchy — elastic means the object RETURNS to original shape. A spring can be elastic; an overstretched spring is inelastic.
Forgetting that Hooke's Law only applies up to the limit of proportionality — beyond this point, doubling the force gives more than double the extension.
Using cm instead of m in Ee = ½ke² — always convert extension to metres before calculating elastic potential energy.
clozePassages: Hooke's Law states that the extension of a spring is directly proportional to the force applied, provided the elastic limit is not exceeded. The relationship is F = ke, where F is force in newtons, k is the spring constant in N/m, and e is extension in metres. The spring constant measures the stiffness of the spring — a larger k means a stiffer spring. Beyond the elastic limit, the spring is permanently deformed.

A spring stores elastic potential energy when stretched or compressed. The energy stored is given by E = ½ke², where k is the spring constant and e is the extension. When released, this stored energy is converted to kinetic energy. Elastic materials return to their original shape when the force is removed. Inelastic (plastic) deformation is permanent — the material does not return to its original shape after the force is removed.

Hooke's Law applies to elastic objects up to the elastic limit. A graph of force against extension is a straight line with gradient equal to the spring constant. Beyond the elastic limit, the line curves — the extension increases more rapidly for the same force. This graph can be used to determine whether the material obeys Hooke's Law and to calculate the spring constant. Materials that obey Hooke's Law are said to be elastic.

Motion.intro: Motion can be described using distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration. Distance-time and velocity-time graphs are essential tools.
Motion.mnemonic: "SUVAT: Silly Unicorns Visit Alien Towns" — s (displacement), u (initial velocity), v (final velocity), a (acceleration), t (time). All five are used in the equations of motion.

sections.title: Key Definitions
sections.text: Motion is described using five key quantities: displacement, speed, velocity, acceleration and time.
points: Speed — distance ÷ time (m/s); scalar; does not specify direction
Velocity — displacement ÷ time (m/s); vector; specifies direction
Acceleration — change in velocity ÷ time (m/s²); vector; can be positive or negative (deceleration)
Average speed — total distance ÷ total time; different from instantaneous speed
Deceleration — negative acceleration; velocity decreasing; e.g. braking car

sections.title: Distance-Time Graphs
sections.text: Distance-time graphs show how position changes with time. The gradient gives the speed at any point.
points: Gradient = speed — steeper line = greater speed
Flat (horizontal) line — stationary; no movement
Straight line — constant speed
Curved line — changing speed (acceleration or deceleration)
Worked example — travel 120 m in 30 s: speed = 120/30 = 4 m/s; gradient on graph = 4

sections.title: Velocity-Time Graphs
sections.text: Velocity-time graphs show how velocity changes with time. Gradient gives acceleration; area gives distance.
points: Gradient = acceleration — a = Δv/Δt; steeper gradient = greater acceleration
Area under graph = distance — for any shape (triangle, rectangle, trapezium)
Flat line — constant velocity (zero acceleration)
Positive gradient — acceleration; negative gradient — deceleration
SUVAT equations — v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as; s = (u+v)/2 × t

sections.title: SUVAT Equations
sections.text: The equations of motion apply to uniform (constant) acceleration. They link the five quantities: s, u, v, a, t.

callout.label: Key Equations
callout.text: v = u + at | s = ut + ½at² | v² = u² + 2as | s = (u+v)/2 × t. (s=displacement, u=initial velocity, v=final velocity, a=acceleration, t=time)

keyTerms.def: Rate of change of velocity: a = Δv/Δt; measured in m/s²; vector quantity
Speed in a given direction — a vector quantity measured in m/s
Distance in a specified direction from a reference point — a vector quantity
Constant rate of change of velocity — SUVAT equations apply
Speed at a particular moment in time — given by gradient of d-t graph at that point
Negative acceleration — velocity decreasing; shown as negative gradient on v-t graph

examTips: v-t graph: gradient = acceleration (use Δv/Δt); area under graph = distance. AQA may ask you to calculate area under a non-rectangular shape — split into triangles and rectangles.
d-t graph: gradient = speed only (NOT acceleration). Flat section = stationary. A curved d-t graph means changing speed.
In SUVAT problems: write down what you know (s, u, v, a, t); identify what is unknown; choose the equation that includes both the unknown and all knowns.
commonMistakes: Reading gradient of a d-t graph as acceleration — gradient of a d-t graph gives SPEED, not acceleration. Only a v-t graph gives acceleration.
Forgetting that the area under a v-t graph gives distance — for a triangle, area = ½ × base × height; for a trapezium, use the trapezium area formula.
Using the final velocity instead of the change in velocity when calculating acceleration — a = Δv/Δt = (v − u)/t, not v/t.
clozePassages: Speed is the distance travelled per unit time, measured in m/s. Velocity is speed in a given direction. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity: a = Δv/Δt. Acceleration is measured in m/s². On a distance-time graph, the gradient gives speed. On a velocity-time graph, the gradient gives acceleration and the area under the graph gives distance. A straight line on a velocity-time graph shows constant acceleration.

The equations of motion (SUVAT equations) apply to uniform acceleration. The key equations are: v = u + at and s = ½(u+v)t, where s is displacement, u is initial velocity, v is final velocity, a is acceleration, and t is time. These equations can be used to solve problems involving objects accelerating uniformly, such as cars braking or objects in free fall (ignoring air resistance).

The velocity of an object changes if its speed changes, its direction changes, or both. Circular motion involves constant change of direction, so the object is always accelerating towards the centre even if its speed is constant. This centripetal acceleration is caused by a centripetal force directed towards the centre. Examples include planets orbiting the Sun, cars going around bends, and satellites in orbit.

Newton's Laws.intro: Newton's three laws of motion describe the relationship between force, mass and acceleration. They are fundamental to understanding how objects move.
Newton's Laws.mnemonic: "1: Inertia keeps things the same. 2: F = ma. 3: Every action has a Reaction" — 1-I, 2-Fma, 3-R. Or: 'Inertia, F=ma, Reaction' for the three laws in order.

sections.title: Newton's First Law
sections.text: Newton's First Law: an object remains at rest or moves at constant velocity unless acted upon by a resultant force.

callout.label: First Law
callout.text: An object remains at rest or moves at constant velocity unless acted upon by a resultant force.

points: Inertia — tendency of objects to resist changes in motion; more massive objects have more inertia
Balanced forces → no acceleration — object stays at rest OR continues at constant velocity
Unbalanced forces needed to change velocity — to speed up, slow down, or change direction
Example — car at constant speed on motorway: engine force = friction + air resistance (balanced)
Space travel — spacecraft in deep space with engines off moves at constant velocity (no friction)

sections.title: Newton's Second Law
sections.text: Newton's Second Law: resultant force equals mass times acceleration. Larger force or smaller mass means greater acceleration.

callout.label: Second Law
callout.text: F = ma (Resultant force = mass × acceleration). Units: F in N, m in kg, a in m/s².

points: F = ma — resultant force (N) = mass (kg) × acceleration (m/s²)
Rearrangements — a = F/m; m = F/a
Larger force — greater acceleration (for same mass)
Larger mass — smaller acceleration (for same force); greater inertia
Worked example — 1200 kg car, resultant force 3600 N: a = F/m = 3600/1200 = 3 m/s²

sections.title: Newton's Third Law
sections.text: Newton's Third Law: for every action force there is an equal and opposite reaction force acting on a different object.

callout.label: Third Law
callout.text: For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. Forces act on DIFFERENT objects — they cannot cancel each other out.

points: Equal and opposite pairs — same magnitude, opposite direction, same type of force
Different objects — each force acts on a different object; they CANNOT cancel each other
Example: walking — foot pushes back on Earth; Earth pushes foot forward (reaction propels person)
Example: rocket — gases pushed down; rocket pushed up by equal and opposite force
Third law ≠ balanced forces — third law pairs act on different objects; balanced forces act on the same object

keyTerms.def: Objects stay at rest or at constant velocity unless a resultant force acts on them
Resultant force = mass × acceleration: F = ma (N = kg × m/s²)
For every action force there is an equal and opposite reaction force acting on a different object
Tendency of an object to resist changes in its state of motion — related to mass
A measure of how difficult it is to accelerate an object — defined as F/a
Unit of force — 1 N is the force that gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s²

examTips: F = ma — rearrange for a = F/m or m = F/a. The resultant force (not just one force) must be used. If two forces act, find the resultant first.
Third law pairs: act on DIFFERENT objects; same type of force; equal magnitude; opposite direction. AQA often asks you to identify the third law pair of a named force.
Balanced forces mean ZERO resultant force, not zero forces. A car at constant speed has many forces acting on it — they are balanced.
commonMistakes: Saying third law forces cancel each other out — they cannot, because they act on different objects. Each object accelerates according to its own resultant force.
Confusing balanced forces (same object, resultant = 0) with Newton's third law pairs (different objects, equal and opposite).
Using the wrong force in F = ma — always use the RESULTANT force, not just the applied force.
clozePassages: Newton's First Law states that an object remains at rest or moves at constant velocity unless acted upon by a resultant force. This means a resultant force is needed to change the velocity of an object — either its speed or direction. Objects resist changes to their state of motion — this is called inertia. The greater the mass, the greater the inertia and the harder it is to change the object's velocity.

Newton's Second Law states that the acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the resultant force and inversely proportional to its mass: F = ma. A larger force produces greater acceleration; a larger mass produces less acceleration for the same force. This equation allows us to calculate the resultant force needed to produce a given acceleration, or the acceleration that results from a given force.

Newton's Third Law states that for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. When object A exerts a force on object B, object B exerts an equal force on A in the opposite direction. These forces act on different objects. For example, when you push on a wall, the wall pushes back on you with the same force. When a rocket expels gas downward, the gas exerts an equal upward thrust on the rocket.

Momentum.intro: Momentum is the product of mass and velocity. It is conserved in all collisions and explosions (in the absence of external forces).
Momentum.mnemonic: "p = mv: Penguins Moving Very fast have lots of momentum" — p is the symbol for momentum, mv is mass × velocity. Conservation: 'Before = After, always.'

sections.title: Momentum Formula
sections.text: Momentum is a vector quantity — it depends on both mass and velocity, so direction matters in calculations.

callout.label: Formula
callout.text: p = m × v (Momentum = mass × velocity). Units: kg m/s. Momentum is a vector quantity.

points: p = mv — momentum (kg m/s) = mass (kg) × velocity (m/s)
Vector quantity — direction must be stated or accounted for with signs (+/−)
Worked example — 1500 kg car at 20 m/s: p = 1500 × 20 = 30 000 kg m/s
Larger momentum — either larger mass or larger velocity (or both)
Units — kg m/s (same as N s); both are acceptable

sections.title: Conservation of Momentum
sections.text: In a closed system (no external forces), the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after.
points: Conservation law — total momentum before = total momentum after (closed system)
Applies to — all collisions and explosions, elastic and inelastic
Collision example — 2 kg ball at 5 m/s hits stationary 3 kg ball; they stick: (2×5) = (2+3)×v → v = 2 m/s
Explosion from rest — initial momentum = 0; products move in opposite directions with equal and opposite momenta
Direction matters — choose positive direction; momentum in opposite direction is negative

sections.title: Impulse and Force
sections.text: Force equals rate of change of momentum. Impulse is the product of force and time, equal to the change in momentum.

callout.label: Force and Momentum
callout.text: F = Δp/Δt (Force = change in momentum ÷ time). Rearranged: F × t = Δp (impulse = change in momentum). Larger time → smaller force for same momentum change — explains crumple zones.

points: F = Δp/Δt — force (N) = change in momentum (kg m/s) ÷ time (s)
Impulse = FΔt = Δp — impulse equals change in momentum; units: N s or kg m/s
Crumple zones — increase collision time → smaller force for same Δp → less injury
Airbags — extend time of impact; reduce force on driver for same change in momentum
Sports applications — 'follow through' in cricket/tennis extends contact time → increases impulse → faster ball

keyTerms.def: Mass × velocity — a vector quantity measured in kg m/s; symbol p
Total momentum before = total momentum after in a closed system (no external forces)
Change in momentum = force × time (N s or kg m/s)
A system with no external forces acting — total momentum is conserved
Collision in which both momentum AND kinetic energy are conserved
Collision in which momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not — some KE converted to thermal energy

examTips: Momentum is conserved in ALL collisions — elastic and inelastic. Kinetic energy is only conserved in elastic collisions. AQA often asks which quantity is always conserved.
Crumple zones increase collision time → smaller force for same change in momentum. This is the key explanation for many car safety features. Use F = Δp/Δt.
In explosion from rest: total initial momentum = 0 (at rest); so momenta of products are equal and opposite (sum = 0). This is a common calculation question.
commonMistakes: Forgetting momentum is a vector — direction matters. If two objects move in opposite directions, one momentum is negative. Add with signs, not just magnitudes.
Saying kinetic energy is conserved in all collisions — kinetic energy is only conserved in perfectly elastic collisions. Most real collisions are inelastic.
Confusing momentum (p = mv) with kinetic energy (KE = ½mv²) — they are different quantities with different formulas and units.
clozePassages: Momentum is defined as mass × velocity and is measured in kg m/s. It is a vector quantity — it has both magnitude and direction. The conservation of momentum states that in a closed system, the total momentum before a collision equals the total momentum after. Momentum is conserved in all collisions and explosions, provided no external forces act. This principle is fundamental to understanding how objects interact.

The impulse of a force is equal to the change in momentum: impulse = F × t = Δ(mv). A large force acting for a short time produces the same change in momentum as a smaller force acting for a longer time. This is why safety features such as airbags and crumple zones are effective — they increase the time of collision, reducing the force. Helmets work on the same principle, extending the time of impact to reduce force on the skull.

Newton's Second Law can be expressed in terms of momentum: F = Δ(mv)/Δt — force equals rate of change of momentum. This is a more general statement than F = ma, which applies only when mass is constant. In an explosion, momentum is conserved — the total momentum is zero before and after, so the products move in opposite directions with equal and opposite momenta. Rockets work by expelling gas backwards, gaining an equal and opposite momentum forwards.

Stopping Distances.intro: The total stopping distance of a vehicle is the sum of thinking distance and braking distance. Both are affected by different factors.
Stopping Distances.mnemonic: "Think Before Braking: Tired Drunk Distracted drivers have longer Thinking distances; Bad roads and Worn brakes make Braking distances worse" — T-D-D for thinking; B-W for braking.

sections.title: Stopping Distance
sections.text: Total stopping distance is split into two parts: thinking distance (during reaction time) and braking distance (during braking).

callout.label: Formula
callout.text: Total stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance.

points: Thinking distance — distance travelled while driver reacts; driver still at full speed
Braking distance — distance travelled while brakes are applied; speed decreases to zero
Total stopping distance — thinking distance + braking distance
Speed affects BOTH — doubling speed doubles thinking distance and quadruples braking distance
Units — typically in metres; reaction time in seconds

sections.title: Factors Affecting Each
sections.text: Thinking distance and braking distance are affected by different factors. Speed affects both.
points: Thinking distance increases with — higher speed, driver tiredness, alcohol, drugs, distraction (phone use)
Braking distance increases with — higher speed, worn tyres, wet/icy road surface, worn/overheated brakes, heavier vehicle
Speed dominates braking — braking distance ∝ v² (kinetic energy ∝ v²); doubling speed quadruples braking distance
Road conditions — ice reduces friction coefficient dramatically; wet roads also reduce grip
Tyre tread — channels water away from contact patch; worn tyres = aquaplaning risk

sections.title: Reaction Time
sections.text: Reaction time is the delay between a stimulus and a response. It determines thinking distance.
points: Typical reaction time — 0.2 to 0.9 seconds for a sober, alert driver
Measurement — ruler drop test (measure distance fallen); computer-based reaction tests
Increased by — alcohol, drugs (prescription and recreational), tiredness, distraction, mobile phone use
Thinking distance calculation — thinking distance = speed × reaction time (e.g. 20 m/s × 0.5 s = 10 m)
Braking force — large braking force = large deceleration; KE removed by friction in brakes (heat generated)

keyTerms.def: Distance travelled during the driver's reaction time — proportional to speed
Distance travelled after brakes are applied until vehicle stops — proportional to speed²
Time between a stimulus and a response — typically 0.2–0.9 s; increased by alcohol, drugs, tiredness
Total distance from hazard detection to full stop: thinking distance + braking distance
Force between brake pads and disc that converts kinetic energy to thermal energy during braking
System that prevents wheel lock during hard braking, maintaining steering control

examTips: Speed affects BOTH thinking distance (proportional to v) AND braking distance (proportional to v²). AQA examiners frequently test whether students know that speed affects both components.
Braking distance ∝ v² because KE = ½mv² must be removed by braking. Doubling speed quadruples braking distance (and therefore total stopping distance approximately quadruples).
In the ruler drop test for reaction time: the further the ruler falls before being caught, the longer the reaction time. Use s = ½gt² to calculate time from distance fallen.
commonMistakes: Saying only road conditions affect stopping distance — road conditions affect braking distance only; reaction time affects thinking distance regardless of road conditions.
Forgetting that speed affects BOTH components of stopping distance — many students only mention braking distance when asked about the effect of speed.
Saying braking distance doubles when speed doubles — braking distance is proportional to v², so doubling speed QUADRUPLES braking distance.
clozePassages: The stopping distance of a vehicle is the distance it travels from when the driver first sees a hazard to when the vehicle stops. It is the sum of the thinking distance (distance travelled during the driver's reaction time) and the braking distance (distance travelled while braking). Reaction time can be increased by tiredness, alcohol, drugs, and distractions. Braking distance depends on speed, road conditions, and vehicle condition.

Thinking distance is directly proportional to speed — if speed doubles, thinking distance doubles. Braking distance is proportional to speed squared — if speed doubles, braking distance quadruples. This is because kinetic energy (which must be removed by braking) is proportional to v². Wet or icy roads reduce friction between tyres and road, increasing braking distance. Worn tyres and brakes also increase braking distance.

During braking, the kinetic energy of the vehicle is converted to thermal energy in the brakes by friction. The braking force needed is related to deceleration by Newton's Second Law (F = ma). Very large braking forces cause rapid deceleration which can be dangerous — anti-lock braking systems (ABS) prevent wheel lock to maintain steering control during emergency stops. Crumple zones in cars increase the time of impact, reducing the force on passengers.
